subject: flamingo
pitch: An elegant flamingo standing tall in shallow water. Candy-pink feathers deepening to coral on the wings, with a flash of black flight feathers at the wing tips, an S-curved neck, a bent beak that is pale pink with a black tip, pale yellow eyes and long rose-coloured legs with knobbly knees and webbed feet.
reasoning:
I need to build a single TypeScript module using the SDK, sticking carefully to the documented helper signatures like createBuilder and joint definitions since I don't have full API docs beyond the reference examples.

For the flamingo, I'm mapping out which primitives to use: chains for joints, sweeps for limbs, extrude/membrane for wings, and part() with scale options for the body shape, while avoiding less-documented helpers like limb() or paint/stripes functions to reduce risk of errors.

Now I'm working through the actual skeleton layout: hips as root joint around y=0.75, long bent legs running from hip through knee to ankle and down to feet near the floor, mirrored on left and right sides at x=±0.09, and a spine chain running from a tail-base point up toward the body for the flamingo's characteristic tilted posture.

I'm then plotting the neck's S-curve as a sequence of control points rising from the base around y=1.0 up to the head near y=1.5, bending forward, back, then forward again to mimic the flamingo's distinctive neck shape, and setting up a catmull-rom chain to connect those points smoothly into the head joint.

Working out joint hierarchy for the head...

Deciding to use b.chain for the neck with a path of points, where chain.at(1) gives a Frame that I can pass directly as the attachment point for head parts, since Frame converts to a position and inherits bone info. For the beak, I'm planning two mandibles — a pale pink upper piece with a black tip and a lower piece — hanging off a jaw joint attached to the head.

Still working out mandible geometry...

I'll use the "aim" option so each part's axis points from a starting location toward an end point, letting me build segments as axis-aligned cylinders regardless of orientation, passing the bone explicitly rather than relying on inference.

For the body, I'm shaping a sphere geometry with a non-uniform scale vector to get an elongated ellipsoid, keeping it mostly horizontal with a slight tilt. I'm settling on a flamingo pink for the body and coral tones for the wing coverts and flight feathers.

For wings I'm extruding a 2D outline shape in the side plane (so the wing lies roughly in the Y-Z plane with X as the thickness direction), defining a feather-shaped outline with a handful of points and mirroring it for the opposite side; I add a separate black extrusion near the tip for flight feathers. I work out the extrusion normal direction from the cross product of the chosen local axes and just accept the uncertainty around the default extrusion depth.

I sketch a tail as a flattened coral sphere near the back of the body, and plan webbed feet using a flattened box or sphere scaled thin, with small toe boxes and knobbly knee spheres at the leg joints.

For the skeleton, I lay out hip, knee, and ankle joints down each leg with approximate coordinates, acknowledging uncertainty about how parent-child joint relationships and chain attachments actually work in this API, and decide to just pass a parent option optimistically. I plan the neck as a chain with an inferred attachment to the spine, and the head as a sphere positioned at the top of the neck.

For eyes I place small pale yellow spheres with tiny dark pupils offset slightly forward, and for the beak I build two mandible segments (pink bases, black hooked tips) using tapered cylinder geometries rotated so their length axis points along the segment direction, via a small helper that computes the midpoint and target point for each piece.

I decide to keep bone assignments explicit only for legs and wings, letting other parts infer their bone from position, and plan leg segments with pink/rose coloring, flattened webbed feet, and small toe segments. With all this reasoned through, I'm ready to write out the final module code and its export.
